MSA DEVIATION REPORT - Nexora Data Solutions, LLC redline (Ashford Merritt, 14 Apr 2025) against Verdantis MSA Template v4.2 and Playbook v3.1
To: Derek Whitfield (AGC) for Priya Narayanan (GC). Privileged. Not for transmission to Nexora or its counsel (Playbook distribution control).

1. BOTTOM LINE
Do not sign on this markup. Nexora's cover email calls most edits "clarifications" and says the cap "remains at 2x." That is wrong. The redline has roughly 160 changed paragraphs. At least 12 are Tier 1 or beyond-fallback Tier 2 and need GC sign-off under Playbook 5.2 and 5.6 (written, not oral). Three Tier 1 items are hard "no" items: BAA timing (6.2), offshore data residency (6.4), and Vendor ownership of models trained on Customer Data (7.1(d)). The data-breach liability triad (Playbook 4) is gutted. The May 30 target is still achievable only if escalation starts now. The GC has committed to a 48-hour turnaround (Playbook 5.7).

2. THRESHOLD ISSUES
(a) Wrong baseline. The redline's underlying text is not our v4.2. It uses different numbering (subprocessors are 6.6, not 6.5). It drops v4.2 text with no tracking: the Customer Data definition no longer covers "data derived from" Customer Data, and v4.2's 6.3 security controls (MFA, 24x7 intrusion monitoring, annual pen-test) and its 7.1(d) Customer Data ownership clause are absent. v4.2 also makes subprocessor consent a matter of "sole discretion" with flow-downs. The header was changed to "Execution Version - April 14, 2025." Require Nexora to re-run its changes against v4.2 (we hold the pen), or run a full compare ourselves, and obtain written confirmation that there are no untracked changes. My comparison was partial. A full compare is needed before any text is agreed.
(b) Playbook cross-reference. The Playbook cites the data breach indemnity as 8.2(b); in v4.2 and the redline it is 8.1(b). The Playbook's $362,500 illustration is also internally inconsistent: six months of fees at $1.45M/yr is $725,000. Neither affects the conclusions.
(c) Email versus markup. Characterized as "minor" or "clarifying": the cap, the super cap, the indemnity ("most serious misconduct" means gross negligence plus a $3M cap), residency, the BAA, IP, and assignment. Not mentioned at all: the 75% early termination fee, the 12-month claims bar, deletion of incident-triggered audits, SOC 2 substitution, the SLA credit cap, subprocessor consent removal, de-identified data retention, the 18% interest rate, the cyber insurance cut, and deletion of the M&A assignment carve-out.
(d) Authority. 45 C.F.R. Parts 160/164 is binding. The Playbook is internal policy only. Governing-law analysis below assumes North Carolina unless noted.

3. DATA-BREACH LIABILITY TRIAD - COMBINED ANALYSIS (Playbook 4.2)
Facts: Year 1 platform fee $1,450,000; platform TCV $4,481,805; with the $385,000 implementation fee, $4,866,805.
- Cap (9.1): 1x fees actually paid in the prior six months, against the template's 2x paid or payable over 12 months. That is below the Playbook's $1M floor early on. It is roughly $115,500 at signing (milestone 1 only), about $0.36-0.48M at month 3, and below $1.1M at month 6, against $2.9M under the template. All three Playbook levers are cut at once: multiplier, lookback, and "actually paid" basis. Net-30 payment lag lowers it further.
- Carve-outs (9.2): confidentiality and data protection carve-outs deleted. Data protection becomes a "Super Cap" of 2x annual fees ($2.9M in Year 1). The fallback is the greater of 3x annual fees ($4.35M) or TCV ($4.48M-$4.87M). Separately, 8.1(b) is capped at a flat $3M, below TCV, which the Playbook says is never acceptable. It is unclear whether the two caps stack or whether 9.2 excludes 8.1(b) claims from the super cap.
- Consequential damages (9.3): the data breach and confidentiality exceptions are deleted. Notification, credit monitoring, OCR and AG penalties, and class costs are likely excluded. "Loss of data" is also excluded for a data host (unchanged from the template, but now fatal). Recovery is effectively direct costs only.
- Trigger (8.1(b)): negligence is replaced by gross negligence. A missed patch or phishing success is typically ordinary negligence, so the indemnity may never trigger.
- Result: best case is about $3M. Realistic early-term recovery is $0.36M-$1.1M of direct damages. The Playbook's catastrophic scenario (14 hospital clients) is $22M-$70M in loss categories. All four Playbook questions (cap, damage types, trigger, defense) resolve against us. Escalate as one package. Position: restore template 8.1(b), 9.1, 9.2, 9.3. Only on GC approval, offer a super cap at the greater of 3x annual fees or TCV for data protection claims, with ordinary negligence, indemnity, IP, and willful misconduct still uncapped.

4. DEVIATION TABLE (Risk: CRITICAL = Tier 1 deal-breaker; HIGH = beyond fallback/GC; MED = AGC authority; LOW)
Disposition key: REJECT, COUNTER, ACCEPT.

6.2/1.4 BAA within 60 days of Effective Date - CRITICAL (Tier 1). REJECT. Under 45 C.F.R. 164.502(e)(1)(ii), 164.504(e) and 164.308(b), PHI cannot go to a subcontractor business associate without a compliant written agreement. Per the memo, PHI migration starts three to four weeks after signing, inside Nexora's 60-day window. Counter: sign Exhibit A BAA concurrently, as a condition to effectiveness. Fallback (GC only): BAA later, with a binding condition precedent that no PHI is disclosed, no PHI-system access is granted, and no PHI services begin until execution. No gap. This also answers Carmen Reeves's question: the BAA is a signing deliverable, and the downstream BAA must be at least as protective as our hospital BAAs.

6.4 Residency to "United States or other jurisdictions Vendor designates" - CRITICAL (Tier 1, no fallback). REJECT. Restore continental US only, for all environments, including access and remote support. Our hospital BAAs require US-only processing. The memo shows Nexora's SOC 2 omits its Singapore environment, where engineers can reach production data. Require written disclosure of all current offshore access and its immediate cessation. Notice and consent are not a cure. Also see 1.21 (Vendor Personnel now include Affiliates), 7.2(b) ("worldwide") and 14.3 (Affiliate assignment): conform all to US-only.

7.1(d) and 7.2(b) Vendor owns models, weights and ML improvements "developed or refined using Customer Data," usable for other customers, and license to Customer Data extended to improving Vendor products - CRITICAL (Tier 1). REJECT. Model weights can encode patient data and cannot be certified free of PHI (Playbook 3.5), and the SOW 3.2(d) and Phase 3 deliverables are Customer models. 7.1(d) conflicts with 7.1(b), which gives Customer the Deliverables. Counter: delete 7.1(d) and limit the 7.2(b) license to performing the Services. Fallback (GC only): Vendor owns only generalized, aggregated, de-identified platform improvements, and only with all four safeguards: no recoverable PHI, no customer-specific models or outputs, written HIPAA Safe Harbor certification (45 C.F.R. 164.514(b)(2)), and a competitor-use covenant. The email's "no customer data included" is not contractually supported, because 7.2(b) authorizes using Customer Data.

6.5 Retention of "de-identified or aggregated" data - CRITICAL/HIGH. REJECT. "Cannot reasonably be used to identify" is not the 164.514(b) standard (Safe Harbor or Expert Determination), and a business associate may de-identify PHI only if its BAA allows it (164.502(d), 164.504(e)(2)(i)). Our hospital BAAs likely prohibit it; confirm. Accept the 60-day return window only as a trade for stronger exit terms (the SOW currently provides a 30-day deletion certification). The "commercially standard format" change is acceptable if it matches SOW formats (CSV/JSON/Parquet).

6.6 Subprocessor consent replaced by notice - HIGH. COUNTER. Restore prior written consent and flow-down of BAA terms (164.504(e)(2)(ii)(D)); US-only; a 30-day list update plus objection is insufficient with no veto. Fallback (GC input needed; not a Playbook position): 30-day notice, objection right, termination without fee if unresolved, US-only and BAA flow-down mandatory.

8.1(b) Gross negligence plus $3M cap - CRITICAL (Tier 1). REJECT. Playbook: no fallback on the negligence standard. 8.1(a): "at its sole cost" is fine. Exclusions (i)-(iii) are acceptable only if "combination" excludes integrations contemplated by the SOW or documentation (Verdantis integrates by design). Add the missing remedies (procure, replace, refund). 8.2(d) Customer indemnity for the "content, accuracy or legality" of Customer Data - HIGH. COUNTER: delete, or limit to Customer's own violation of law, fault-based and excluding Vendor's processing. 3.3 (added rep that Customer holds "all consents") - MED/HIGH. COUNTER: limit to consents Customer must obtain under HIPAA for the disclosure, "to Customer's knowledge."

9.1 Cap 1x/6-month/"actually paid" - HIGH, becomes CRITICAL with 9.2/9.3. REJECT. Counter: restore 2x paid or payable over 12 months. Fallback (AGC): 1.5x paid or payable over at least 12 months. Because the early-term cap is below $1M, a floor ("greater of the formula or $2.9M") would address it. Reject the added "regardless of form of action" and "failure of essential purpose" language in 9.4 unless the carve-outs are restored.

9.5 12-month claims bar, accruing "regardless of when the party knew" - HIGH (Tier 2 beyond fallback). REJECT. NC gives three years for written contracts (N.C. Gen. Stat. 1-52(1)), and breaches are often discovered after 6-12 months. Fallback (GC): 24 months from discovery, excluding data protection/HIPAA, indemnity and IP claims. As drafted it also bars third-party indemnity claims.

10.2 Convenience termination Customer-only and 75% ETF - HIGH (Tier 2 beyond fallback). REJECT. The Playbook preferred schedule is 25% of remaining fees in Year 1, 15% in Year 2, then 0%. The maximum fallback is 50%, declining, and total payments must stay below 75% of TCV. Modeled on the $4,866,805 total: terminating at the end of Year 1 costs a 75% fee of about $2.27M, for $4.11M total paid (84% of TCV). At the end of Year 2 the fee is $1.15M and total paid $4.48M (92%). Both exceed the 75% cap and need GC. Restore bilateral termination and the SOW-level fee reference (the SOW says "as set forth in the Agreement"; the template said "in the SOW"). Preserve the SOW 7.4 chronic-SLA exit without a fee. Fallback: 50% maximum, declining. Note that 4.3 and 14.10 may override SOW 7.4.

10.3 Cure 45 days plus open-ended extension - MED/HIGH. COUNTER. Accept 45 days (fallback). Extension must have a hard outer limit: 30 additional days (75 total), commenced and diligently pursued. Keep 10 days for payment defaults.

10.5(b),(e),(f) Immediate acceleration of all invoices, all Customer licenses terminate immediately, and a survival list that omits Section 6 and Section 3 - HIGH. COUNTER: acceleration only for undisputed amounts. Licenses continue through the data export and transition period (SOW). Add Sections 3, 6 and the BAA to survival.

11.2/11.1 SOC 2 in lieu of audit, incident-triggered audits (at Vendor expense) deleted - CRITICAL (Tier 1 for PHI). REJECT. The Singapore scope gap means a SOC 2 report gives no assurance over the environment where the highest-risk access occurs. Playbook fallback (AGC): SOC 2 may satisfy only the annual scheduled audit, if it covers all environments including development, staging and DR, if Customer can audit if the report shows exceptions, and if incident-triggered audits (Vendor expense) are preserved in full. Accept the calendar-year, business-hours, and minimal-disruption edits. 11.3: accept the confidentiality qualifier only if it cannot limit access to any environment holding Customer Data. Exhibit B: insist on SOC 2 report scope verification and keep annual pen-testing ("periodic" is rejected).

13.1/13.2/13.3/13.4 California law, binding arbitration before the "Western Arbitration Council," seated in San Francisco, no punitive damages, mediation step removed - HIGH (Tier 2 beyond fallback). REJECT. All Playbook "escalation" triggers are met: vendor home-city seat, damages restriction, non-standard body (I could not verify that this body exists or is nationally recognized). Counter: NC law (fallback: Delaware); mediation for 60 days, then Durham courts. Fallback arbitration (GC): JAMS or AAA/ICDR seated in Durham or a neutral venue, no damages restrictions, court injunctive relief preserved. The jury waiver deletion matters little if arbitration is rejected; if litigation returns, restore it. California predispute jury waivers are generally unenforceable (Grafton Partners v. Superior Court, 36 Cal.4th 944 (2005)), another reason to resist California law.

14.3 Assignment: M&A carve-out deleted - HIGH (Tier 2). COUNTER. Restore the carve-out, with the assignee assuming in writing. Fallback: assignee not a direct competitor, 30-day notice, creditworthiness, consent not unreasonably withheld for M&A. The Affiliate carve-out also lets Vendor move PHI to an affiliate: require US-only and BAA coverage.

4.3 SLA credit cap 5% ($72,500/yr) plus "commercially reasonable efforts" (4.1) and third-party downtime exclusion (4.4(e)) - HIGH (Tier 2 below 10%). COUNTER. A single 94% month under the SOW credit table is $36,250, so two such months exhaust the cap. Fallback: not less than 15% ($217,500), sole-remedy limited to routine misses, and a termination right for chronic failure. Below 10% requires GC. Restore "shall meet" in 4.1 and monthly reports in 4.2 (the SOW provides monthly reports). Delete 4.4(e) or limit it to causes Vendor could not reasonably prevent (Vendor's subprocessors remain its responsibility).

12.1 Cyber insurance $10M to $5M - HIGH (Tier 2; $5M is the absolute floor for PHI). COUNTER: $10M. Fallback (AGC): $7.5M, since TCV is under $5M. $5M or less needs GC. Certificate of insurance before execution, not within ten business days after (the memo says limits remain unconfirmed). Accept the 30-day cancellation notice. "Where commercially available" for additional insured status - MED, counter: delete or narrow.

5.6 Trade secret survival fixed at five years; general confidentiality reduced to three years - HIGH. Three years for general information is within fallback (ACCEPT). Trade secrets must be indefinite (REJECT). Add indefinite survival for PHI and Customer Data. 5.1 makes only Vendor's pricing, architecture and algorithms confidential: COUNTER to mutual, and v4.2 treats Customer Data as Confidential Information. 5.5: Vendor retention under "standard document retention policies" - COUNTER: no retention of PHI or Customer Data.

6.3 Incident notice 24 to 48 hours - HIGH (not a tier in the Playbook). COUNTER: keep 24 hours. Nexora's incident response plan only says "without unreasonable delay," and Verdantis must notify downstream hospital clients. Accept 48 hours only if hospital BAA deadlines permit (45 C.F.R. 164.410 sets only an outer limit of 60 days, so check the contracts). Define "Security Incident" by reference to the BAA.

6.1/3.2(b) "commercially reasonable" safeguards; the GDPR-style "rights and freedoms of natural persons" clause - MED/HIGH. COUNTER: restore "appropriate" and delete the GDPR language (wrong regime and dilutes the HIPAA Security Rule). "Commercially reasonable" is acceptable only if tied to NIST CSF, HITRUST CSF or ISO 27001/27002 (Playbook fallback). 3.2(a) "generally accepted practices": ACCEPT. 3.2(e) knowledge qualifier on non-infringement: COUNTER, delete. 3.4: restore "this Agreement, any SOW and the BAA" instead of "this Section 3."

2.3 Net 30, 18% interest, 15-day dispute notice - LOW/MED. Net 30 is Tier 3: ACCEPT, as a trade (SOW says Net 45 from receipt; conform). Interest at 1.5% a month exceeds the 12% GC threshold: COUNTER at lesser of WSJ prime + 2% or 10%, undisputed amounts only, starting 15 days after the due date, with a savings clause. Dispute notice: 15 days is too short and risks waiver; counter 45 days, with no waiver.

13.5 Force majeure - MED. ACCEPT pandemic/epidemic and sanctions. Termination trigger 120 days: COUNTER at 90 (beyond 90 needs GC). The automatic SOW extension is acceptable only for events up to 30 days. Delete "cyberattacks on critical infrastructure not specific to Vendor's systems" (a ransomware-by-proxy excuse), exclude security and BAA obligations from excuse, and abate fees during suspension.

2.1/2.2/14.10/2.4 - MED. "Subject to Customer's compliance" and "commercially reasonable efforts": REJECT (conditions performance). 14.10 puts the BAA last, contradicting 6.2 (BAA controls on PHI): COUNTER, BAA first for PHI. Align 2.2 with SOW express-supersession and SLA terms. 2.4 taxes: conform to the SOW (excludes gross receipts and franchise taxes).

1.x/14.x - LOW/MED. NDA incorporation (recital, 14.1): COUNTER, delete or subordinate to Section 5 and the BAA (we have not reviewed the NDA). 7.3 Feedback perpetual, irrevocable license: COUNTER to v4.2 (no Customer Data, PHI or Confidential Information, no attribution). 14.11 Publicity: REJECT, no logo use without written consent (hospital client sensitivity). 14.8: restore indemnitee third-party beneficiary rights. 1.21: delete "Affiliates" and "subcontractors" unless bound by Section 6 and the BAA. Accept: 1.3, 1.5 ("source code"), 1.9 (limit to SOW escalators, 3%), 1.11, 1.15, 14.2, 14.5, 14.6, 14.9, 3.1, 8.3, 13.4, 5.2, 5.4 (conforming and neutral).

5. NEGOTIATION STRATEGY
Escalate to the GC now: 6.2, 6.4, 7.1(d), 8.1(b), 9.2/9.3 (as one package), 11.2, 6.5, 6.6 (Tier 1); and 9.1, 9.5, 10.2, 13.x, 14.3, 4.3, 5.6, 12.1, 13.5 (Tier 2 beyond fallback). Concessions available within AGC authority: Net 30, pandemic/sanctions force majeure, 45-day cure with 75-day cap, calendar-year audit cadence, SOC 2 as a supplement, three-year general confidentiality, "generally accepted practices," electronic signatures, 1.5x cap. Call with Greystone and Sienna Caldwell; reserve the CEO-level call for Tier 1 items. Consult Hannah Prescott (Ridgeline) on ML/de-identification IP. Ask Nexora to correct its cover-email characterizations in writing. Consult Carmen Reeves and Jared Koh (Playbook 5.4) on ETF, SLA and payment terms. Keep the Playbook confidential.

6. LIMITS
Authorities were taken from the Playbook and my knowledge and were not independently fetched or Shepardized. The redline-to-template comparison was partial. Current HIPAA rulemaking (the January 2025 Security Rule proposal) status should be confirmed.
